set1.io: Define asthma
set1.q: Patients with asthma have the most difficulty with which part of breathing?
opts: Getting air out of the lungs

Correct. Asthma makes expiration difficult; air is trapped behind the narrowed airways and the lungs hyperinflate. That is why the history asks whether symptoms come with breathing in or out, and why a prolonged expiratory phase tracks the obstruction.
Drawing air into the lungs

Inspiration is relatively preserved in asthma. The narrowed airways limit expiration, so patients struggle to empty the lungs and trap air, causing hyperinflation. Tell: difficulty drawing air in, especially with stridor, points to an upper airway problem in the differential.
reversed direction or value
Moving oxygen across the alveolar wall

Gas diffusion across the alveolar wall is not the asthma defect. Bronchoconstriction, edema and secretions narrow the airways so air cannot get out easily. Tell: a diffusion problem shows up as a low diffusing capacity, which is the emphysema pattern, not asthma.
confused mechanism or drug class
Coordinating the diaphragm with the chest wall

Asthma is not a neuromuscular coordination problem. Airway narrowing makes expiration hard and traps air. Tell: the asthma patient during an attack uses accessory muscles and leans forward because the airways, not the muscles, are the obstruction.
confused mechanism or drug class

set1.io: Define, describe, and discuss aspergillosis as it relates to asthma.
set1.q: Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis is best described as which process?
opts: Invasive fungal infection of healthy lungs

The process is a hypersensitivity, an allergic reaction, not invasion of normal lungs, and it occurs almost exclusively in people with asthma or cystic fibrosis. Tell: the word allergic in the name signals an immune over-reaction rather than tissue invasion.
confused mechanism or drug class
Bacterial pneumonia after influenza

Post-influenza pneumonia is a bacterial infection. Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis is a hypersensitivity reaction to the Aspergillus mold. Tell: Aspergillus is a fungus, and the disease is driven by antibodies rather than infection.
competing diagnosis
Occupational reaction to workplace chemicals

That describes occupational asthma, which improves away from work. Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis is hypersensitivity to Aspergillus. Tell: the trigger here is a mold, not a chemical, and it occurs in patients who already have asthma or cystic fibrosis.
competing diagnosis
Hypersensitivity reaction to Aspergillus species

Correct. Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis is a hypersensitivity reaction to Aspergillus species, mainly Aspergillus fumigatus, occurring almost exclusively in asthma or cystic fibrosis; exposure provokes a vigorous immunoglobulin E and G response and acute asthma symptoms.

set1.q: Occupational asthma classically shows which pattern?
opts: Symptoms peak in a monthly cycle

Symptoms at predictable times of the menstrual cycle describe catamenial asthma. Occupational asthma tracks the work schedule, improving on weekends and vacations. Tell: a monthly rhythm points to the menstrual cycle; a weekly rhythm points to work.
competing diagnosis
Symptoms improve on weekends and vacations

Correct. Occupational sensitizers, mostly chemicals, cause asthma independent of atopy, and symptoms improve during weekends and vacations away from the workplace. Onset may come weeks or years after exposure and sensitization.
Symptoms worsen on weekends at home

The workplace pattern is the reverse: symptoms improve away from work on weekends and vacations because the sensitizing agent is absent. Tell: worse at home suggests a home allergen such as dust mites or pet dander, not an occupational agent.
reversed direction or value
Sensitization requires pre-existing atopy

Occupational sensitization is independent of atopy, so a non-atopic worker can develop it. Its clue is improvement on weekends and vacations. Tell: atopy is the risk factor for extrinsic asthma, not a requirement for workplace sensitization.
reversed direction or value

set1.q: Which findings are common in intrinsic asthma?
opts: Nasal polyps and aspirin sensitivity

Correct. Intrinsic asthma is of later onset, usually more severe and persistent, commonly has nasal polyps, and may be aspirin sensitive. Its allergy tests are negative with a normal immunoglobulin E.
Elevated immunoglobulin E and positive skin tests

Elevated immunoglobulin E and positive skin tests mark extrinsic, atopic asthma. Intrinsic asthma has normal immunoglobulin E and negative tests, with nasal polyps common. Tell: intrinsic means no allergic trigger, so the allergy markers stay normal.
reversed direction or value
Mild symptoms that remit in adolescence

Intrinsic asthma starts in adulthood and is usually more severe and persistent, so mild disease remitting in adolescence does not fit. Tell: remission in adolescence describes the course of childhood asthma, not the adult-onset intrinsic form.
wrong stage or severity
Symptoms tied to the menstrual cycle

Symptoms at predictable times of the menstrual cycle describe catamenial asthma. Intrinsic asthma brings nasal polyps and possible aspirin sensitivity. Tell: catamenial asthma is defined by timing, intrinsic asthma by its negative allergy workup.
competing diagnosis

set1.q: Why must allergen immunotherapy for asthma be given in a controlled environment?
opts: It must be infused over several hours

Infusion time is not the concern. The risk of inducing bronchoconstriction, which may need urgent treatment, is why a controlled environment is needed. Tell: the setting is chosen for safety, to treat a reaction, not for convenience.
adjacent fact
It causes oral candidiasis

Thrush is an inhaled corticosteroid effect. Immunotherapy exposes the patient to the allergen and risks bronchoconstriction. Tell: the danger of giving an allergen to an allergic patient is an asthma attack, not a mouth infection.
confused mechanism or drug class
It works best with many allergens at once

It is most useful as single-allergen immunotherapy, the opposite of combining many allergens. The controlled setting is for the bronchoconstriction risk. Tell: the stated best use is narrow, one allergen at a time.
reversed direction or value
It can induce bronchoconstriction

Correct. Immunotherapy may be considered for patients with allergic triggers and reduces symptoms, most usefully as single-allergen therapy, but it must be given in a controlled environment because it risks inducing bronchoconstriction that may need urgent treatment.

set1.q: What is the preferred first-line long-term treatment for persistent asthma?
opts: Theophylline

Theophylline is rarely used because of its narrow toxic-therapeutic range and toxicity. Inhaled corticosteroids are the preferred first-line controller. Tell: a drug kept for rare use because of toxicity cannot be the preferred first choice.
adjacent fact
A leukotriene modifier alone

Leukotriene modifiers are less effective than inhaled corticosteroids as monotherapy and are mainly add-on therapy or used for exercise-induced bronchospasm. Tell: the comparison drug in that statement, the inhaled corticosteroid, is the first-line choice.
adjacent fact
An inhaled corticosteroid

Correct. Inhaled corticosteroids are the preferred first-line treatment for persistent asthma; most patients respond to twice-daily use, though the maximum response may take months. They reduce the airway inflammation that defines the disease.
A long-acting beta-2 agonist alone

A long-acting beta-2 agonist has no anti-inflammatory effect and should not be used as monotherapy; it is added to an inhaled corticosteroid. Tell: first-line controller therapy has to treat inflammation, which a bronchodilator alone does not.
ruled out by a stated finding

set1.q: Which medications act as asthma triggers and should be avoided in patients with asthma?
opts: Albuterol and levalbuterol

These are short-acting beta-2 agonists that relax airway smooth muscle and relieve symptoms. Aspirin and beta blockers are the medication triggers. Tell: an agonist at the beta-2 receptor opens the airway, while a beta blocker can close it.
reversed direction or value
Aspirin and beta blockers

Correct. Aspirin and beta blockers are the medication triggers listed and should be avoided in patients with asthma; exercise is listed with them as a trigger. Patients with true aspirin sensitivity should also avoid non-selective anti-inflammatory drugs.
Inhaled corticosteroids and leukotriene modifiers

These are controller medications that reduce inflammation or block leukotrienes, not triggers. The medications to avoid are aspirin and beta blockers. Tell: controllers prevent attacks; triggers provoke them.
reversed direction or value
Celecoxib and meloxicam

These selective anti-inflammatory drugs may be used even in aspirin-sensitive asthma, so they are the safe alternatives. The triggers to avoid are aspirin and beta blockers. Tell: selective agents are what aspirin-sensitive patients switch to.
reversed direction or value

set1.q: Daily symptoms, daily rescue inhaler use, and some limitation of activity fit which severity class?
opts: Severe persistent

Severe persistent asthma has symptoms throughout the day, rescue use several times a day and extreme limitation, with lung function below 60% predicted. Tell: some limitation is moderate; extreme limitation is severe.
wrong stage or severity
Moderate persistent

Correct. Daily symptoms, daily short-acting beta-2 agonist use, night awakenings more than once a week but not nightly, some limitation, and a forced expiratory volume in 1 second between 60% and 80% predicted define moderate persistent asthma.
Intermittent
Intermittent asthma has symptoms and rescue use on 2 or fewer days a week with no interference, so daily symptoms are far too frequent. Tell: daily anything rules out intermittent asthma.
wrong stage or severity
Mild persistent

Mild persistent asthma has symptoms on more than 2 days a week but not daily, with only minor limitation. Daily symptoms and daily rescue use push the patient to moderate. Tell: the word daily is the line between mild and moderate persistent asthma.
wrong stage or severity

set1.io: List the components of patient education in treating asthma, including use of peak flow meters, metered-dose inhalers, nebulizers.
set1.q: How long can the maximum response to an inhaled corticosteroid take?
opts: Hours

Hours is still too fast for the maximum response; inhaled corticosteroids may take months to reach full effect. Tell: patients who expect results within hours may stop the controller too early, a compliance trap.
reversed direction or value
Days
Days is shorter than stated. The maximum response may take months. Tell: early improvement may come sooner, but the question asks about the maximum response, which is a matter of months.
reversed direction or value
Months

Correct. Most patients respond to twice-daily inhaled corticosteroid dosing, but the maximum response may take months, so patients should keep taking it daily rather than expect the quick relief of a rescue inhaler.
Minutes

Minutes describes a short-acting bronchodilator, which relaxes smooth muscle quickly. The full effect of an inhaled corticosteroid can take months. Tell: anti-inflammatory controllers work slowly, which is why they are taken every day, not as needed.
confused mechanism or drug class

set1.q: Which statement about allergen avoidance and the development of asthma is accurate?
opts: Strict avoidance in infancy prevents asthma

Avoidance does not lower the risk of developing asthma, and early exposure may instead build tolerance. Tell: avoidance is a treatment for existing asthma (remove the trigger), not a prevention strategy for new asthma.
common lay belief
Avoidance doubles the risk of atopic dermatitis

No such effect is taught. The stated point is that allergen avoidance does not reduce the risk of developing asthma, while early exposure may be protective. Tell: the claim invents a specific harm the evidence never describes.
confused mechanism or drug class
Avoidance cures established asthma

Trigger avoidance and environmental control reduce symptoms in established asthma but do not cure a chronic inflammatory disease, and avoidance does not prevent asthma from developing. Tell: avoidance is one non-pharmacologic measure used alongside medications, not a cure.
adjacent fact
Avoidance does not reduce the risk of developing asthma

Correct. Inhaled allergens are common triggers and are implicated in sensitization, yet avoiding them does not reduce the risk of developing asthma; early exposure may even be protective by building tolerance. Avoidance still helps patients who already have asthma by removing triggers.

set1.q: Airway hyper-responsiveness in asthma is best described as which response?
opts: Loss of elastic recoil that collapses airways on expiration

Loss of elastic recoil collapsing the airways on expiration is the emphysema mechanism. Asthma's hyper-responsiveness is excessive bronchoconstriction to a trigger. Tell: loss of recoil comes from destroyed alveolar walls and does not reverse after a bronchodilator.
competing diagnosis
Excessive bronchoconstriction to a trigger a normal airway ignores

Correct. Hyper-responsiveness is excessive bronchoconstriction in response to a trigger that would have no effect on a normal airway, and the degree of hyper-responsiveness is linked to how often symptoms occur. The key elements are a trigger, an exaggerated response and a normal airway that would not react.
Fixed narrowing that does not change with any trigger

Fixed narrowing that ignores triggers is the opposite of hyper-responsiveness. The asthmatic airway over-reacts to triggers, and its narrowing largely reverses. Tell: hyper-responsiveness is about a reaction to a trigger, so a description with no trigger response cannot fit.
reversed direction or value
Bronchodilation that overshoots after exposure to a trigger

The abnormal response is bronchoconstriction, not dilation: a trigger a normal airway tolerates makes the asthmatic airway clamp down. Bronchodilation is what rescue medication produces. Tell: if the airway dilated, wheezing and airflow limitation would not follow the trigger.
reversed direction or value

set1.q: Which body mass index is linked to more frequent and harder-to-control asthma?
opts: Below 18

A low body mass index is not the listed risk. Obesity, a body mass index above 30, makes asthma more frequent and harder to control. Tell: the risk sits at the high end of weight, so an underweight value points the wrong way.
reversed direction or value
Between 18 and 25

A normal body mass index is not a risk factor. The endogenous risk factor is obesity, a body mass index above 30, which makes asthma both more frequent and harder to control. Tell: this range is the healthy weight band.
reversed direction or value
Between 25 and 27

This overweight band is below the threshold given. Asthma is more frequent, and harder to control, once the body mass index is above 30. Tell: the cutoff is the obesity line of 30, not the overweight range.
adjacent fact
Above 30

Correct. Asthma is more frequent in people with a body mass index above 30, and their symptoms are more difficult to control; the mechanism is unknown. Obesity is listed among the endogenous risk factors with genetics, atopy and early viral infection.

set1.q: Which pain medication may be used by a patient with aspirin-sensitive asthma?
opts: Naproxen

Naproxen is non-selective and should be avoided in aspirin-sensitive asthma; a selective agent such as celecoxib may be used. Tell: naproxen sits on the avoid list with ibuprofen, diclofenac and indomethacin.
ruled out by a stated finding
Indomethacin

Indomethacin is on the avoid list of non-selective anti-inflammatory drugs; the selective agents celecoxib and meloxicam may be used. Tell: every drug on the avoid list is non-selective, so pick the selective one.
ruled out by a stated finding
Celecoxib

Correct. Patients with aspirin-sensitive asthma should avoid non-selective anti-inflammatory drugs (diclofenac, ibuprofen, naproxen, indomethacin) but may use selective agents such as celecoxib or meloxicam.
Ibuprofen

Ibuprofen is a non-selective anti-inflammatory drug, which aspirin-sensitive patients should avoid because of cross-reactivity; celecoxib is selective. Tell: the safe agents are the selective ones, celecoxib and meloxicam.
ruled out by a stated finding

set1.q: How many exacerbations requiring oral corticosteroids in the past year may classify a patient as persistent despite minimal impairment?
opts: With no steroid-requiring exacerbations, the risk domain does not push the patient into persistent asthma; 2 or more a year does. Tell: zero exacerbations fits the intermittent risk row of 0 to 1 a year.
reversed direction or value
Zero to one exacerbation a year fits intermittent asthma in the risk domain; it takes 2 or more to count as persistent. Tell: a single steroid burst in a year is still within the intermittent row.
wrong stage or severity
2 or more

Correct. Patients with 2 or more exacerbations requiring oral systemic corticosteroids in the past year may be considered the same as patients with persistent asthma, even without the impairment levels of persistent disease. The risk domain can override a quiet impairment picture.
5 or more
Five is far above the threshold. Two or more steroid-requiring exacerbations in a year already count as persistent. Tell: waiting for five would leave a high-risk patient undertreated.
reversed direction or value

set1.q: Which form of tobacco exposure has evidence as an asthma risk factor?
opts: Maternal smoking

Correct. Under passive cigarette smoke there is evidence that maternal smoking is a risk factor for asthma, although its effect is difficult to separate from the increased risk of respiratory infections in exposed children.
Smoking by a relative who lives elsewhere

Exposure from a relative who lives in another home is not the factor with evidence; passive exposure needs shared air. The evidence is for maternal smoking. Tell: the risk factor is the closest, most constant exposure in early life.
adjacent fact
Nicotine replacement patches

Nicotine replacement is a smoking-cessation aid that delivers nicotine without smoke. The risk factor with evidence is maternal smoking. Tell: a patch produces no smoke, so it cannot be a passive smoke exposure.
confused mechanism or drug class
Smoking that began after age 60

The evidence for asthma concerns passive smoke exposure, with maternal smoking as the risk factor, rather than the patient's own smoking. Late-onset smoking is a risk factor for chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Tell: look for the passive exposure, which here is maternal smoking.
competing diagnosis

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), patient education, and prognosis of asthma.
set1.q: Which feature is found in intrinsic but not extrinsic asthma?
opts: Negative skin tests, normal immunoglobulin E

Correct. Intrinsic asthma, about 10% of patients, has negative skin allergy tests and a normal serum immunoglobulin E, starts later in adulthood, and is usually more severe and persistent. Extrinsic asthma is allergen-triggered and atopic.
Attacks set off by allergen exposure

Triggering by allergens defines extrinsic asthma, the most common form. Intrinsic asthma is not triggered by allergens and is not atopic. Tell: if allergens set off the attacks, the skin tests would be positive, which is the extrinsic picture.
reversed direction or value
A different underlying airway pathology

The pathology is the same in extrinsic and intrinsic asthma; what differs is the allergic profile. Intrinsic asthma has negative skin tests and normal immunoglobulin E. Tell: the distinction is made with allergy testing, not with a biopsy.
adjacent fact
Onset at the peak age of 3 years

Childhood onset is typical of asthma overall. Intrinsic asthma has later, adult onset, and its distinguishing tests are negative skin tests and normal immunoglobulin E. Tell: intrinsic is the adult-onset, non-allergic form.
reversed direction or value

set1.q: What does a chest radiograph usually show in asthma?
opts: Lobar consolidation

Consolidation suggests pneumonia, an alveolar filling process. In asthma the radiograph is usually normal or shows hyperinflation. Tell: asthma traps air and makes the lungs look darker and larger, while consolidation makes a lobe white.
competing diagnosis
Pleural effusions

Effusions are not part of asthma; they suggest heart failure, infection or malignancy. The asthma radiograph is usually normal or hyperinflated. Tell: an effusion sits outside the lung in the pleural space, far from asthma's airway disease.
competing diagnosis
Normal lungs or hyperinflation

Correct. The chest radiograph in asthma is usually normal or may show hyperinflation from air trapping, so it supports rather than makes the diagnosis and mainly helps exclude other causes of symptoms.
Bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy

Hilar lymphadenopathy is not an asthma finding and suggests a granulomatous or malignant process. The asthma radiograph is usually normal or shows hyperinflation. Tell: asthma is an airway disease that leaves the hila and lymph nodes alone.
competing diagnosis

set1.q: At what time of day do asthma symptoms tend to peak?
opts: 3 to 4 in the morning

Correct. Symptoms may be worse at night because of circadian variation in bronchomotor tone and bronchial reactivity, which peaks around 3 to 4 in the morning. Night awakenings are therefore one of the severity measures.
Noon
Midday is not the peak. Circadian variation in bronchial reactivity makes asthma symptoms peak around 3 to 4 in the morning.
reversed direction or value
Late afternoon

Late afternoon is when peak flow is re-measured after the bronchodilator, not when symptoms peak; the circadian peak is around 3 to 4 in the morning. Tell: the afternoon reading is the after-treatment check, while the worst airway tone is overnight.
adjacent fact
Early evening

Early evening is not the circadian peak. Bronchial reactivity peaks around 3 to 4 in the morning, which is why night symptoms are common. Tell: the peak falls in the middle of sleep, so it shows up as night awakenings rather than evening symptoms.
reversed direction or value

set1.q: Exercise-induced bronchospasm typically peaks how long after exercise?
opts: 1 to 2 minutes
Onset can come during exercise or within 3 minutes after it, but the peak is later, at 10 to 15 minutes. Tell: 1 to 2 minutes fits the onset window, not the peak.
adjacent fact
10 to 15 minutes

Correct. Exercise-induced bronchospasm begins during or within 3 minutes after exercise, peaks in 10 to 15 minutes and resolves by 60 minutes. That short, predictable window is why a short-acting inhaler before exercise works.
60 minutes
By 60 minutes the episode has resolved, so an hour is the end point rather than the peak, which comes at 10 to 15 minutes. Tell: an hour marks when the airway has recovered, not its worst point.
adjacent fact
4 to 6 hours
Exercise-induced bronchospasm is brief: it peaks in 10 to 15 minutes and resolves within an hour. Tell: hours-long symptoms would suggest an ordinary exacerbation, not exercise-induced bronchospasm.
reversed direction or value

set1.q: Which three components establish the diagnosis of asthma?
opts: Symptom response to an oral corticosteroid trial

A steroid trial is not how asthma is diagnosed; systemic steroids are reserved for exacerbations and severe disease. The diagnosis needs history, physical examination and objective lung function. Tell: the objective test is spirometry before and after a bronchodilator, not a drug trial.
common lay belief
History, physical exam, and objective lung function

Correct. Asthma is diagnosed from the history, the physical examination and an objective measurement of lung function. The objective measure matters because the exam can be normal between attacks, and it feeds both the diagnostic criteria and the severity classification.
History, chest radiograph, and allergy testing

A chest radiograph is usually normal or shows hyperinflation, and allergy testing identifies triggers; neither measures airflow. The diagnosis needs an objective lung function test such as spirometry. Tell: only an airflow measurement can show the reversible obstruction that defines asthma.
adjacent fact
Physical exam, serum immunoglobulin E, and sputum culture

Immunoglobulin E separates extrinsic from intrinsic asthma and sputum culture looks for infection; neither establishes asthma. The diagnosis rests on history, physical exam and objective lung function. Tell: a normal immunoglobulin E does not exclude asthma, since intrinsic asthma occurs with a normal immunoglobulin E level.
confused mechanism or drug class

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), patient education, and prognosis of asthma.
set1.q: Compared with beta-2 agonists, how do inhaled anticholinergics such as tiotropium perform in asthma?
opts: More effective, with fast onset

Anticholinergics are less effective than beta-2 agonists and slow in onset, because they block only the cholinergic reflex component. Tell: a fast, more effective agent is the beta-2 agonist profile, which is why it is the rescue drug.
reversed direction or value
Equally effective, with heavy side effects

Little or no systemic absorption gives anticholinergics few side effects, and they are less effective than beta-2 agonists. Tell: poor absorption is the reason for their mild side-effect profile, the opposite of heavy side effects.
reversed direction or value
Equally effective as rescue drugs

Their slow onset makes them unsuitable as rescue drugs, and they are less effective than beta-2 agonists. A short-acting beta-2 agonist is the rescue agent. Tell: a slow-onset drug cannot rescue an attack.
wrong stage or severity
Less effective, with slow onset

Correct. Anticholinergics such as tiotropium inhibit only the cholinergic reflex component of bronchoconstriction and mucus secretion, so they are less effective than beta-2 agonists and slow in onset; little systemic absorption leaves few side effects.

set1.q: Which examination finding correlates with the degree of airway obstruction in asthma?
opts: A pericardial friction rub

A friction rub is a pericarditis sign and says nothing about airway obstruction. A prolonged expiratory phase correlates with obstruction in asthma. Tell: a rub is a heart sound tied to the cardiac cycle, not to breathing out.
competing diagnosis
Inspiratory crackles at the bases

Basilar inspiratory crackles suggest alveolar fluid or fibrosis, not asthma's airway obstruction. The finding that tracks obstruction is a prolonged expiratory phase. Tell: asthma's findings cluster on expiration, while crackles here are inspiratory.
competing diagnosis
A shortened expiratory phase

Obstruction lengthens expiration rather than shortening it, because air leaves slowly through narrowed airways. A prolonged expiratory phase correlates with the obstruction. Tell: the more narrowed the airway, the longer it takes to breathe out.
reversed direction or value
A prolonged expiratory phase

Correct. A prolonged expiratory phase during normal respiration correlates with obstruction, because air takes longer to leave through narrowed airways. In severe exacerbations wheezing may disappear, leaving decreased breath sounds with prolonged expiration.

set1.q: Which set of symptoms is typical of asthma?
opts: Constant fever, night sweats, and weight loss

Constant systemic symptoms such as fever, night sweats and weight loss are not asthma features and suggest infection or malignancy. Asthma is episodic wheezing, dyspnea, chest tightness and cough. Tell: asthma comes and goes with triggers rather than producing steady systemic illness.
competing diagnosis
Pleuritic chest pain relieved by leaning forward

Sharp chest pain relieved by leaning forward is a pericarditis pattern. Asthma presents with episodic wheezing, dyspnea, chest tightness and cough. Tell: asthma patients may lean forward to breathe during an attack, but chest tightness, not positional pain, is the complaint.
competing diagnosis
Stridor that is loudest on inspiration

Inspiratory stridor points to an upper airway problem, such as vocal fold dysfunction or a laryngotracheal mass, which is in the differential. Asthma causes episodic expiratory wheezing, dyspnea and cough. Tell: asthma's noise is on expiration, not inspiration.
competing diagnosis
Episodic wheezing, dyspnea, chest tightness, and cough

Correct. Asthma symptoms vary but include episodic wheezing, dyspnea, chest tightness, cough and sputum production, occurring spontaneously or after a trigger and often worse at night. The episodic pattern reflects reversible obstruction.

set1.q: Which is an upper airway disorder in the differential diagnosis of asthma?
opts: Vocal fold dysfunction

Correct. Upper airway mimics include vocal fold paralysis or dysfunction, foreign body aspiration and laryngotracheal masses; lower airway mimics include chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, bronchiectasis and cystic fibrosis.
Bronchiectasis

Bronchiectasis is a lower airway disorder in the differential, grouped with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and cystic fibrosis. Vocal fold dysfunction is the upper airway mimic here. Tell: bronchiectasis affects the bronchi, below the larynx.
adjacent fact
Cystic fibrosis

Cystic fibrosis is listed among the lower airway mimics, with bronchiectasis and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Vocal fold dysfunction is the upper airway one. Tell: upper airway means larynx and above, where the vocal folds sit.
adjacent fact
Conversion disorder

Conversion disorder is a psychiatric cause in the differential, with emotional laryngeal wheezing and rarely malingering, not an upper airway disorder. Tell: the upper airway group is structural or functional problems of the larynx and trachea.
adjacent fact

set1.io: Develop a treatment plan for patients with asthma based on symptoms and physical examination.
set1.q: What is the key to success in asthma treatment?
opts: Daily oral corticosteroids

Systemic corticosteroids are for exacerbations or refractory disease at the minimum dose, with side effects such as osteoporosis and ulcers; they are not the key to success. Compliance is. Tell: daily systemic steroids conflict with the goal of minimizing adverse effects.
wrong stage or severity
Patient compliance

Correct. The treatment goals are minimal chronic symptoms, no exacerbations or emergency visits, normal lung function and activity, and minimal drug side effects, and patient compliance is the key to reaching them. Non-compliance is also the most common reason for refractory symptoms.
Allergen immunotherapy

Immunotherapy is an add-on for selected patients with allergic triggers, given in a controlled setting because it can induce bronchoconstriction. Compliance is named as the key to treatment success. Tell: a niche add-on cannot be the key for every patient.
adjacent fact
Avoiding physical activity

A goal of asthma treatment is no limitation on physical activity, so avoiding activity runs against the plan. Exercise symptoms are prevented with medication instead. Tell: the goals list protects activity rather than restricting it.
reversed direction or value

set1.q: What percentage of patients with asthma become worse with aspirin?
opts: 1 to 5%
Correct. About 1 to 5% of asthmatics become worse with aspirin, through a genetic predisposition that increases inflammatory mediators. Aspirin is among the medication triggers to avoid.
This overstates the share. Aspirin sensitivity affects about 1 to 5% of people with asthma. Tell: aspirin sensitivity is 1% to 5%, not 10% to 15%.
adjacent fact
This is far too high; about 1 to 5% of asthmatics worsen with aspirin. Tell: aspirin sensitivity is a small subgroup, not a quarter of patients.
reversed direction or value

Half of patients is a large overstatement; aspirin-sensitive asthma is 1 to 5% of asthmatics. Tell: if half of patients reacted, aspirin sensitivity would be a defining feature of asthma rather than a subtype.
reversed direction or value

set1.io: List the components of patient education in treating asthma, including use of peak flow meters, metered-dose inhalers, nebulizers.
set1.q: On a written asthma action plan, the green zone corresponds to a peak flow of at least what percent of personal best?
opts: Fifty percent is the lower edge of the yellow zone; below it is the red, medical-alert zone. Green starts at 80% of personal best. Tell: 50% is a warning boundary, not the doing-well zone.
wrong stage or severity
Sixty percent falls in the yellow zone of 50% to 79%, when asthma is getting worse and quick-relief medicine is added. Green requires 80% or more. Tell: anything in the 50s to 70s is yellow.
wrong stage or severity

Correct. The green zone, doing well, is a peak flow of 80% or more of personal best with long-term controllers taken daily; the yellow zone is 50% to 79%, when quick-relief medicine is added, and the red zone is below 50%, a medical alert.
Ninety-five percent is not required; 80% or more of personal best is the green zone. Tell: demanding near-perfect readings would put well-controlled patients in the yellow zone needlessly.
reversed direction or value

set1.io: Identify medical care strategies for patients with asthma in the following patient populations. 1. adolescent 2. adult 3. elderly
set1.q: Which statement about asthma across the life span is accurate?
opts: Remission in adolescence is permanent

An adolescent remission is not necessarily permanent: asthma may return in adulthood. Tell: the course described is remit-and-return, so a quiet adolescence does not rule out adult symptoms or the need to reassess later.
reversed direction or value
It worsens in severity with each decade of life

Severity rarely varies for a patient, and mild asthma rarely becomes severe. The life-span pattern is presentation at any age, possible remission in adolescence and possible return in adulthood. Tell: severity is stable; it is symptoms that can come and go.
reversed direction or value
It may remit in adolescence and return in adulthood

Correct. Asthma presents at any age with a peak at 3 years, may become asymptomatic during adolescence, and may return in adulthood. A teenager whose asthma went quiet is not cured and should still be asked about childhood symptoms later in life.
It cannot begin after childhood

Asthma can present at any age; intrinsic asthma in particular has later, adult onset and is usually more severe. Tell: the peak age of presentation is 3 years, but a peak is not a limit, and adult-onset disease is a recognized type.
common lay belief

set1.io: Describe how PFTs are utilized to aid in the diagnosis of pulmonary diseases and monitoring of patients with those diseases
set1.q: When is bronchial provocation testing useful in suspected asthma?
opts: When spirometry already shows reversibility

A clear bronchodilator response already strongly supports asthma, so provocation adds little. It is used when spirometry is not diagnostic. Tell: provocation fills the gap when the routine test is inconclusive, not when it has answered the question.
wrong stage or severity
When the 1-second volume is below 50% predicted

Provocation is not recommended when the forced expiratory volume in 1 second is below 65% predicted, so a value under 50% rules it out. Tell: provoking bronchospasm in a patient with already poor function is unsafe.
ruled out by a stated finding
During an acute exacerbation

Provoking bronchospasm during an exacerbation is unsafe and pointless, since the airway is already narrowed. Provocation is used when baseline spirometry is not diagnostic. Tell: a challenge test is an outpatient test for a stable patient with unclear spirometry.
wrong stage or severity
When spirometry is not diagnostic

Correct. Bronchial provocation with a methacholine or histamine challenge is useful when spirometry is not diagnostic; an exercise challenge is used if exercise-induced bronchospasm is suspected. It is not recommended when the forced expiratory volume in 1 second is below 65% predicted.

set1.io: List the components of patient education in treating asthma, including use of peak flow meters, metered-dose inhalers, nebulizers.
set1.q: What change between morning and afternoon peak flow readings indicates poor asthma control?
opts: Five percent is ordinary variation and does not signal poor control. A 20% change, morning to afternoon or day to day, does. Tell: the poor-control line is a fifth of the reading, not a few percent.
reversed direction or value

Ten percent is not the cutoff; poor control is a 20% change in morning-to-afternoon or day-to-day readings. Tell: 10% resembles the bronchodilator-response figures in spirometry, a different test and a different threshold.
reversed direction or value
Correct. A 20% change between morning and afternoon peak flow measurements, or a 20% change from day to day, indicates poor asthma control and should prompt a review of the treatment plan.
Fifty percent is not the variability threshold; a 20% swing already indicates poor control. Tell: 20% is the swing between readings that matters.
adjacent fact

set2.io: Develop a treatment plan for patients with asthma based on symptoms and physical examination.
set2.q: Which features define intermittent asthma?
opts: Symptoms over 2 days a week, night waking 3 to 4 times a month

Symptoms on more than 2 days a week (but not daily) with 3 to 4 night awakenings a month define mild persistent asthma. Tell: crossing the 2-days-a-week line moves a patient out of intermittent into persistent asthma.
wrong stage or severity
Daily symptoms, night waking more than once a week

Daily symptoms with night awakenings more than once a week but not nightly define moderate persistent asthma. Tell: daily symptoms and daily rescue use are the moderate markers, far beyond the intermittent limit of 2 days a week.
wrong stage or severity
Symptoms throughout the day, night waking often 7 times a week

Symptoms throughout the day and night awakenings often 7 times a week define severe persistent asthma, with extremely limited activity. Tell: nightly waking is the severe marker; intermittent asthma wakes the patient 2 or fewer times a month.
wrong stage or severity
Symptoms 2 or fewer days a week, night waking 2 or fewer times a month

Correct. Intermittent asthma has symptoms and rescue use on 2 or fewer days a week, night awakenings 2 or fewer times a month, no interference with normal activity, and normal lung function between exacerbations.

set2.io: Develop a treatment plan for patients with asthma based on symptoms and physical examination.
set2.q: When features of a patient's asthma fall into different severity categories, which category is assigned?
opts: The least severe category with any feature
Choosing the mildest category would undertreat the patient. The rule is the most severe category in which any feature occurs. Tell: classification errs toward the highest feature, never the lowest.
reversed direction or value
The category set by lung function alone

Lung function is one impairment feature among several, alongside symptoms, night awakenings, rescue use and interference. The most severe category in which any feature falls decides. Tell: a normal spirometry result does not cancel daily symptoms.
adjacent fact
The most severe category with any feature

Correct. Severity is assigned to the most severe category in which any feature occurs, after assessing impairment over the previous 2 to 4 weeks with spirometry. One severe feature is enough to move the patient up.
The category that holds most of the features

Severity does not go by majority vote. It is assigned to the most severe category in which any feature occurs. Tell: a patient with mostly mild features but one moderate feature is moderate, because undertreating the worst feature is the risk.
common lay belief

set2.io: Describe how PFTs are utilized to aid in the diagnosis of pulmonary diseases and monitoring of patients with those diseases
set2.q: Below what forced expiratory volume in 1 second is bronchial provocation testing not recommended?
opts: 40% predicted

Forty percent is lower than the cutoff given; provocation is already avoided once the forced expiratory volume in 1 second falls below 65% predicted. Tell: waiting until 40% would allow testing in patients with far too little reserve.
reversed direction or value
65% predicted

Correct. Bronchial provocation deliberately triggers bronchospasm with methacholine or histamine, so it is not recommended if the forced expiratory volume in 1 second is below 65% predicted. Below that, the airway has too little reserve.
80% predicted

Eighty percent is the normal-function line in the severity table, not the provocation cutoff, which is 65% predicted. Tell: 80% separates mild from moderate persistent asthma; 65% is the safety line for a challenge test.
adjacent fact
90% predicted

Ninety percent is not the threshold and would exclude nearly everyone. Provocation is not recommended when the forced expiratory volume in 1 second is under 65% predicted. Tell: the cutoff sits well below normal function, at 65%.
reversed direction or value

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), patient education, and prognosis of asthma.
set2.q: What is cardiac asthma?
opts: Asthma triggered by a beta blocker

Beta blockers are a medication trigger of true asthma and should be avoided in patients with asthma. Cardiac asthma is wheezing produced by decompensated heart failure. Tell: the beta blocker worsens real asthma; cardiac asthma is not asthma at all.
adjacent fact
Palpitations from short-acting bronchodilators

Palpitations and tremor are side effects of beta-2 agonists. Cardiac asthma is a heart-failure cause of wheezing. Tell: cardiac asthma describes a cause of wheeze, not a drug side effect felt in the chest.
confused mechanism or drug class
Asthma that causes right heart strain

Right heart strain from lung disease is cor pulmonale, a complication of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Cardiac asthma runs the other way: a failing heart produces wheezing. Tell: in cardiac asthma the heart causes the wheeze, not the lungs strain the heart.
reversed direction or value
Wheezing caused by decompensated heart failure

Correct. Cardiac asthma is wheezing caused by decompensated heart failure rather than by asthma itself. A new wheeze in a patient with heart disease should prompt evaluation of the heart, not just bronchodilators.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), patient education, and prognosis of asthma.
set2.q: Which early-life infection may be associated with later development of asthma?
opts: Streptococcal pharyngitis in childhood

Streptococcal pharyngitis is a bacterial throat infection and is not listed. The endogenous factor is early viral infection, specifically respiratory syncytial virus in infancy. Tell: the association is viral and lower-respiratory, not bacterial and pharyngeal.
confused mechanism or drug class
Childhood exposure to farm germs

Early germ exposure appears in the hygiene hypothesis as possibly protective, because it helps the immune system develop. Respiratory syncytial virus in infancy is the infection linked to later asthma. Tell: the hygiene hypothesis predicts less asthma with more early germ exposure.
reversed direction or value
Respiratory syncytial virus in infancy

Correct. Early viral infection, particularly respiratory syncytial virus in infancy, may have an association with later asthma development. In someone who already has asthma, the same virus is also a trigger of exacerbations.
Aspergillus fumigatus in infancy

Aspergillus causes allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis, a hypersensitivity seen almost exclusively in people who already have asthma or cystic fibrosis. Tell: aspergillosis complicates existing asthma, while respiratory syncytial virus in infancy is the early-life association.
adjacent fact

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), patient education, and prognosis of asthma.
set2.q: Which finding is listed as a toxic effect of theophylline?
opts: Hyperkalemia
Theophylline toxicity causes hypokalemia, a low potassium, not a high one. Tell: the listed electrolyte change is a fall in potassium, paired with a rise in glucose.
reversed direction or value
Hypoglycemia
Theophylline toxicity causes hyperglycemia, not hypoglycemia. Tell: the glucose and potassium move in opposite directions in theophylline toxicity, glucose up and potassium down.
reversed direction or value
Seizure

Correct. Theophylline toxic effects include nausea, vomiting, tachyarrhythmias, headache, seizure, hyperglycemia and hypokalemia; insomnia, dyspepsia and reflux are its ordinary side effects. Its narrow toxic-therapeutic range makes it rarely used.
Oral candidiasis

Oral thrush is a local inhaled corticosteroid effect, prevented with a spacer and rinsing, not theophylline toxicity. Tell: theophylline is a systemic drug whose toxicity hits the brain, heart and metabolism, not the mouth.
confused mechanism or drug class

set2.io: Define asthma
set2.q: Which description defines asthma?
opts: Restrictive disorder that limits filling of the lungs

Asthma is obstructive: the problem is getting air out of the lungs, which traps air and hyperinflates them. A restrictive disorder limits filling, the opposite pattern. Tell: asthma lowers the ratio of the 1-second volume to vital capacity, which a restrictive disorder leaves normal.
reversed direction or value
Chronic inflammatory airway disorder with reversible obstruction

Correct. Asthma is a chronic inflammatory airway disorder whose airflow obstruction is reversible, producing recurrent breathlessness and wheezing and difficulty getting air out of the lungs. Some long-standing cases develop irreversible obstruction, but reversibility is the defining feature.
Chronic infection of the airways with fixed obstruction

Asthma is inflammatory, not infectious, and its obstruction reverses rather than staying fixed. Viral infections are triggers that worsen existing asthma. Tell: an infection-based definition with fixed obstruction cannot explain why asthma improves after a bronchodilator.
confused mechanism or drug class
Destruction of alveolar walls with permanent air trapping

Permanent destruction of alveolar walls is emphysema, a subtype of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Asthma narrows the airways through inflammation and bronchoconstriction that can reverse. Tell: the word permanent points away from asthma's reversible obstruction.
competing diagnosis

set2.io: Develop a treatment plan for patients with asthma based on symptoms and physical examination.
set2.q: Why should a long-acting beta-2 agonist not be used as monotherapy in asthma?
opts: It causes oral candidiasis

Thrush is an inhaled corticosteroid effect, not a beta-agonist effect. The long-acting agent lacks anti-inflammatory action, which is why it is paired with a steroid. Tell: beta agonists cause tremor and palpitations, not thrush.
confused mechanism or drug class
It cannot be given by inhaler

Long-acting beta-2 agonists are inhaled. They are not used alone because they have no anti-inflammatory effect. Tell: the problem is what the drug does not do, treat inflammation, not how it is delivered.
confused mechanism or drug class
It has no anti-inflammatory effect

Correct. A long-acting beta-2 agonist such as salmeterol or olodaterol bronchodilates for up to 12 hours but has no anti-inflammatory effect, so it is combined with an inhaled corticosteroid, often allowing control at a lower steroid dose.
It lasts too short a time to help

Duration is not the problem; it gives bronchodilation for up to 12 hours. The issue is the lack of anti-inflammatory effect in an inflammatory disease. Tell: short duration describes the 3-to-6-hour rescue agents, not this class.
reversed direction or value

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), patient education, and prognosis of asthma.
set2.q: Which group of processes limits air movement in asthma?
opts: Bronchoconstriction, airway edema, and vascular congestion

Correct. Asthma limits air movement through bronchoconstriction, airway edema and vascular congestion, with occlusion of the airway lumen by secretions in some cases. All of these narrow the airway itself, which is why the obstruction can reverse.
Alveolar destruction, bullae, and loss of recoil

Alveolar destruction, bullae and loss of elastic recoil describe emphysema, where airspaces are permanently enlarged. Asthma narrows the airway by bronchoconstriction, edema, congestion and secretions. Tell: bullae and loss of recoil are parenchymal changes, not airway-wall changes.
competing diagnosis
Pleural fibrosis, chest wall stiffness, and weakness

These limit filling of the lungs, a restrictive pattern. Asthma is obstructive: bronchoconstriction, airway edema, vascular congestion and secretions narrow the airway. Tell: restriction shrinks lung volumes, whereas asthma traps air and can hyperinflate the lungs.
confused mechanism or drug class
Pulmonary edema, alveolar fluid, and cardiomegaly

Alveolar fluid from decompensated heart failure causes cardiac asthma, a mimic that wheezes for a different reason. True asthma narrows the airway through bronchoconstriction, edema and congestion of the airway wall. Tell: cardiomegaly and alveolar fluid point to the heart, not the airway.
competing diagnosis

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), patient education, and prognosis of asthma.
set2.q: Between exacerbations, the physical examination of a patient with asthma is often what?
opts: Marked by digital clubbing

Clubbing is not an asthma finding; it suggests another chronic lung or heart disease. Between exacerbations the asthma examination may be entirely normal. Tell: asthma's reversible airway disease leaves no permanent marks such as clubbing.
competing diagnosis
Marked by a barrel chest

A barrel chest from chronic hyperinflation is the chronic obstructive pulmonary disease picture. The asthma exam is often normal between attacks. Tell: a persistent barrel chest implies fixed air trapping, which asthma usually does not have.
competing diagnosis
Normal

Correct. The examination may be normal between exacerbations, which is why an objective lung function measurement is needed for the diagnosis. Extrinsic asthma may still show nasal mucosal swelling, increased secretions, eczema or nasal polyps.
Marked by fixed wheezing

Wheezing usually appears during exacerbations; between attacks the exam is often normal because the obstruction is reversible. Tell: fixed, constant findings suggest irreversible disease such as chronic obstructive pulmonary disease rather than asthma between attacks.
wrong stage or severity

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), patient education, and prognosis of asthma.
set2.q: Which signs show increased work of breathing during an asthma exacerbation?
opts: Facial flushing, rhinorrhea, and conjunctival irritation

These are features of an aspirin-sensitive reaction, not signs of increased work of breathing. Work-of-breathing signs are accessory muscle use, leaning forward and hunched shoulders. Tell: flushing and runny nose describe the trigger reaction, not the breathing effort.
adjacent fact
Clubbing, cyanosis, and edema of the ankles

These are chronic signs of long-standing lung or heart disease, not the acute work-of-breathing signs of an exacerbation. Tell: work of breathing is seen in how the patient breathes and sits, accessory muscles and a forward-leaning, hunched posture.
wrong stage or severity
Accessory muscle use, leaning forward, hunched shoulders

Correct. Increased work of breathing during an exacerbation shows as accessory muscle use, leaning forward and hunched shoulders. These signs mean the patient is struggling to move air through narrowed airways.
Slow deep breaths with a relaxed posture

Slow, relaxed breathing is the opposite of increased work of breathing. An exacerbation brings accessory muscle use, leaning forward and hunched shoulders. Tell: a relaxed posture says the patient is not struggling, which rules out a significant exacerbation.
reversed direction or value

set2.io: Identify medical care strategies for patients with asthma in the following patient populations. 1. adolescent 2. adult 3. elderly
set2.q: How is exercise-induced bronchospasm best prevented?
opts: Regular inhaled corticosteroid use

Correct. Exercise-induced bronchospasm is treated with an inhaled short-acting beta-2 agonist before exercise and is best prevented with regular inhaled corticosteroid use. It is common in children and adolescents, so this keeps teenagers in sport.
Avoiding exercise entirely
A goal of asthma care is no limitation on activity; medication, not avoidance, prevents the bronchospasm. Tell: the treatment plan protects participation in sport rather than removing it.
common lay belief
Oral theophylline before games

Theophylline is rarely used because of toxicity and is not the exercise strategy. Regular inhaled corticosteroids best prevent exercise-induced bronchospasm, with a short-acting inhaler before exercise. Tell: the pre-exercise drug is inhaled, not an oral methylxanthine.
adjacent fact
A long-acting beta-2 agonist alone

A long-acting beta-2 agonist must not be used as monotherapy because it has no anti-inflammatory effect. Regular inhaled corticosteroids are the best prevention. Tell: any long-acting agent in asthma must ride with an inhaled corticosteroid.
ruled out by a stated finding

set2.io: Describe how PFTs are utilized to aid in the diagnosis of pulmonary diseases and monitoring of patients with those diseases
set2.q: Airflow reduction in asthma lowers which set of measurements?
opts: Total lung capacity, residual volume, and diffusion

These are not the measurements listed as falling. Lung volumes rise with air trapping rather than fall, and diffusion is a parenchymal measure. Asthma lowers the 1-second volume, its ratio to forced vital capacity, and peak flow. Tell: asthma's numbers are all expiratory flow measures.
adjacent fact
Arterial oxygen, carbon dioxide, and bicarbonate

Blood gas values do not define airflow reduction. Spirometry and peak flow do: the forced expiratory volume in 1 second, its ratio, and peak expiratory flow all fall. Tell: airflow is measured at the mouth with a spirometer or peak flow meter, not in the blood.
confused mechanism or drug class
Inspiratory flow, tidal volume, and breathing rate

Asthma limits expiration, so the measures that fall are expiratory: the forced expiratory volume in 1 second, its ratio to forced vital capacity, and peak expiratory flow. Tell: every asthma measurement on the list is taken while the patient blows out, not breathes in.
reversed direction or value
Expiratory volume in 1 second, its ratio, and peak flow

Correct. Reduced airflow lowers the forced expiratory volume in 1 second, the ratio of that volume to forced vital capacity, and the peak expiratory flow. These are all expiratory measures, matching asthma's difficulty getting air out.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), patient education, and prognosis of asthma.
set2.q: Which feature raises the risk of death from asthma?
opts: Onset of symptoms before age 3

Early onset is common and is not listed as a death risk. The risks are poor control, missing or skipped inhaled corticosteroids, and prior near-fatal admissions. Tell: the death risks describe how asthma is controlled, not when it began.
adjacent fact
Regular use of an inhaled corticosteroid

Regular inhaled corticosteroid use lowers the risk; the absence of an inhaled corticosteroid, or poor compliance with it, raises it. Widespread inhaled corticosteroid use is why asthma deaths are falling. Tell: this is the protective factor written as a risk.
reversed direction or value
Symptoms that resolve during adolescence

Asthma may become asymptomatic in adolescence and return in adulthood, but remission is not a death risk. Prior near-fatal admissions and poor control are. Tell: a quiet period means less disease activity, the opposite of the high-risk features.
adjacent fact
Previous admission for a near-fatal attack

Correct. Risk of death rises with poorly controlled asthma (frequent bronchodilator use), no inhaled corticosteroid or poor compliance with it, and previous admissions for near-fatal attacks. A past near-fatal attack is one of the listed markers.

set2.io: Describe how PFTs are utilized to aid in the diagnosis of pulmonary diseases and monitoring of patients with those diseases
set2.q: Which spirometry pattern before a bronchodilator signals airflow limitation in asthma?
opts: Reduced 1-second volume and reduced ratio

Correct. Before a bronchodilator, airflow limitation shows as a reduced forced expiratory volume in 1 second and a reduced ratio of that volume to forced vital capacity. Improvement after the bronchodilator then supports asthma.
Normal ratio, reduced vital capacity

A normal ratio with a low forced vital capacity suggests restriction, a filling problem. Asthma's obstruction lowers both the 1-second volume and the ratio. Tell: in obstruction the 1-second volume falls more than the vital capacity, so the ratio drops.
competing diagnosis
Increased 1-second volume

Obstruction lowers, not raises, the forced expiratory volume in 1 second, and the ratio to forced vital capacity falls too. Tell: air leaves the narrowed airway slowly, so less of it gets out in the first second.
reversed direction or value
Normal values, lower after dilator

Values improve after a bronchodilator in asthma rather than fall, and before it the 1-second volume and the ratio are reduced. Tell: a positive response is a rise of 12% or more in the 1-second volume, not a drop.
reversed direction or value

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), patient education, and prognosis of asthma.
set2.q: Asthma deaths are declining in affluent countries because of the widespread use of which therapy?
opts: Allergen immunotherapy

Immunotherapy may reduce symptoms in selected patients with allergic triggers and must be given in a controlled setting, so it is not widespread. The decline follows inhaled corticosteroid use. Tell: the decline is attributed to inhaled corticosteroids.
adjacent fact
Inhaled corticosteroids

Correct. Death from asthma is uncommon and declining in affluent countries, credited to widespread use of inhaled corticosteroids, the anti-inflammatory controller. The flip side is that having no inhaled corticosteroid, or poor compliance with it, raises the risk of death.
Short-acting bronchodilators

Short-acting bronchodilators relieve symptoms, but frequent use marks poorly controlled asthma with a higher risk of death. The decline is credited to inhaled corticosteroids. Tell: rescue drugs treat attacks; only an anti-inflammatory controller changes the underlying disease.
confused mechanism or drug class
Oral theophylline

Theophylline is rarely used because of its narrow toxic-therapeutic range and toxicity such as seizures and arrhythmias, so it cannot explain falling deaths. Inhaled corticosteroids can. Tell: a drug that is rarely used is not a widespread therapy.
adjacent fact

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), patient education, and prognosis of asthma.
set2.q: Which statement about mast cell stabilizers such as cromolyn is accurate?
opts: They are the preferred rescue medication

They cannot relieve symptoms once present, so they cannot be rescue drugs; a short-acting beta-2 agonist is. Tell: prevention-only drugs are taken before the trigger, while a rescue drug works after symptoms start.
reversed direction or value
They are reserved for severe persistent asthma

They help mild persistent or exercise-induced asthma. Severe disease needs stronger controllers such as inhaled corticosteroids with a long-acting agent. Tell: these are mild-disease preventers, not severe-disease therapy.
wrong stage or severity
They have a narrow toxic-therapeutic range

A narrow toxic-therapeutic range requiring close monitoring describes theophylline, not mast cell stabilizers. Tell: the monitoring warning belongs to the methylxanthine with seizure and arrhythmia toxicity.
confused mechanism or drug class
They do not relieve symptoms once present

Correct. Cromolyn and nedocromil inhibit mast cell activation and eosinophil recruitment; they prevent symptoms and improve function in mild persistent or exercise-induced asthma but do not relieve symptoms once they are present.

set2.io: Develop a treatment plan for patients with asthma based on symptoms and physical examination.
set2.q: Which task belongs to the initial asthma visit rather than a follow-up visit?
opts: Assess and monitor asthma control

Assessing and monitoring control is a follow-up task, after treatment has started; severity is what the initial visit assesses. Tell: severity is judged before treatment, control is judged on treatment.
wrong stage or severity
Adjust medications as needed

Adjusting medication happens at follow-up once control is known. The initial visit assesses severity and starts therapy. Tell: there is nothing to adjust until the first medication has been started and its effect seen.
wrong stage or severity
Review the action plan and update it
Reviewing and updating the plan is a follow-up task; the initial visit develops the written action plan in the first place. Tell: a plan has to exist before it can be reviewed.
wrong stage or severity
Assess asthma severity

Correct. The initial visit diagnoses asthma, assesses severity, starts medication and demonstrates its use, develops a written action plan and schedules follow-up. Follow-up visits then assess and monitor control, review compliance and adjust medications.

set2.io: Develop a treatment plan for patients with asthma based on symptoms and physical examination.
set2.q: What is the most common reason for poor symptom control in refractory asthma?
opts: Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis

Aspergillosis is a hypersensitivity seen in asthma that causes exacerbations, but it is not the most common reason for poor control; non-compliance is. Tell: the commonest cause is behavioral, not a second disease.
competing diagnosis
Exercise-induced bronchospasm

Exercise-induced bronchospasm is predictable and prevented with pre-exercise and regular controller therapy. Non-compliance is the usual cause of poor control. Tell: exercise symptoms come and go with activity, while refractory asthma means poor control despite treatment.
competing diagnosis
Non-compliance

Correct. Refractory asthma takes two forms, persistent symptoms with poor lung function or normal function with severe exacerbations; non-compliance is the most common reason for poor symptom control, and steroid-resistant asthma is very uncommon.
Steroid-resistant asthma
Steroid-resistant asthma is very uncommon. Non-compliance is the most common reason for poor symptom control. Tell: before blaming the drug, check whether the patient is actually taking it correctly.
reversed direction or value

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), patient education, and prognosis of asthma.
set2.q: During a severe exacerbation, why can the absence of wheezing be worrying?
opts: It shows bronchodilator toxicity

Beta-2 agonist side effects are tremor and palpitations, not loss of wheeze. A quiet chest in a severe attack signals minimal airflow. Tell: drug toxicity changes the pulse and hands, while a silent chest reflects how little air is getting through.
confused mechanism or drug class
Airflow may be too low to wheeze

Correct. Wheezing may be absent in severe exacerbations; the patient may have only decreased breath sounds with prolonged expiration because so little air is moving. A quiet chest in a struggling patient is a sign of severity, not improvement.
It shows the attack has ended

A silent chest in a patient still working hard to breathe does not mean the attack is over. Wheezing can vanish in severe exacerbations, leaving only decreased breath sounds. Tell: improvement brings easier breathing as well as less wheeze, not a struggling patient with a quiet chest.
common lay belief
It shows the cause is cardiac

Cardiac asthma causes wheezing from heart failure, so it would add wheeze rather than remove it. The absence of wheeze in an asthma attack signals very little air movement. Tell: a quiet chest is about airflow volume, not about the heart.
competing diagnosis

set2.io: Describe how PFTs are utilized to aid in the diagnosis of pulmonary diseases and monitoring of patients with those diseases
set2.q: How is spirometry best performed when asthma is suspected?
opts: Before and after a bronchodilator

Correct. Spirometry measures the volume of air exhaled over time; the best results come from measuring before and after a short-acting bronchodilator, so reversibility can be shown. It is repeated annually to monitor progression.
After a week of oral corticosteroids

A steroid course is not part of the test and would blur the baseline. Spirometry is done before and after a short-acting bronchodilator to show reversibility. Tell: the comparison is minutes apart around a bronchodilator dose, not a week apart around steroids.
adjacent fact
During sleep at 3 to 4 in the morning

Spirometry needs a coached, maximal effort while awake, because results depend on patient effort. It is performed before and after a short-acting bronchodilator. Tell: 3 to 4 in the morning is when symptoms peak, not when the test is done.
confused mechanism or drug class
After exercise to provoke symptoms

An exercise challenge is a separate provocation test used when exercise-induced bronchospasm is suspected. Routine spirometry is pre- and post-bronchodilator. Tell: provocation tries to cause bronchospasm, while standard spirometry tries to show it reverses.
adjacent fact

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), patient education, and prognosis of asthma.
set2.q: Which psychiatric conditions appear in the differential diagnosis of asthma?
opts: Generalized anxiety and panic disorder

These are not the conditions listed. The psychiatric differential is conversion disorder, emotional laryngeal wheezing and, rarely, malingering or factitious disorder. Tell: the listed mimics produce a wheeze-like noise, not just a feeling of breathlessness.
adjacent fact
Bipolar disorder and schizophrenia

Neither is listed as an asthma mimic. Conversion disorder and emotional laryngeal wheezing are, with malingering rarely. Tell: the mimics are conditions that can produce laryngeal noise, not primary mood or psychotic disorders.
common lay belief
Depression and insomnia
Neither is listed as an asthma mimic. Tell: the psychiatric differential is conversion disorder, emotional laryngeal wheezing and, rarely, malingering or factitious disorder.
adjacent fact
Conversion and emotional laryngeal wheeze

Correct. Psychiatric causes in the differential are conversion disorders, emotional laryngeal wheezing and, rarely, malingering or factitious disorder. They can mimic asthma, which is one reason an objective lung function test is part of the diagnosis.

set2.q: On an asthma action plan, which finding is a danger sign that calls for the hospital or an ambulance now?
opts: Blue lips or fingernails

Correct. The danger signs on the action plan are trouble walking and talking because of shortness of breath, and blue lips or fingernails; the patient takes quick-relief medicine and goes to the hospital or calls an ambulance now.
Peak flow at 85% of best
Eighty-five percent of personal best is the green zone, doing well. Blue lips or fingernails are a danger sign. Tell: any reading of 80% or more is green, the opposite of a danger sign.
wrong stage or severity
Cough that comes with exercise

Cough with exercise suggests exercise-induced symptoms managed with a short-acting inhaler before exercise, not a danger sign. Tell: danger signs show failing oxygenation or effort, such as blue lips or inability to talk.
wrong stage or severity
Mild morning chest tightness

Mild tightness fits the yellow zone at most, managed by adding quick-relief medicine. The danger signs are blue lips or fingernails and trouble walking or talking. Tell: mild symptoms and danger signs sit at opposite ends of the plan.
wrong stage or severity

set2.q: Which viruses are listed as triggers of asthma exacerbations?
opts: Hepatitis B, hepatitis C, and immunodeficiency virus

These blood-borne viruses do not infect the airway and are not asthma triggers. Respiratory viruses are: influenza, rhinovirus, respiratory syncytial virus and coronavirus. Tell: asthma triggers reach the airway, so they are respiratory viruses.
confused mechanism or drug class
Herpes simplex, varicella, and Epstein-Barr virus

None of these is on the trigger list. The viral triggers are respiratory: influenza, rhinovirus, respiratory syncytial virus and coronavirus. Tell: the listed viruses all cause upper respiratory infections.
adjacent fact
Measles, mumps, and rubella

These are not listed as asthma triggers. The respiratory viruses influenza, rhinovirus, respiratory syncytial virus and coronavirus are. Tell: the common cold and flu viruses, not the childhood rash illnesses, set off asthma.
adjacent fact
Influenza, rhinovirus, and other respiratory viruses

Correct. Viral infections trigger exacerbations by a poorly understood mechanism; the list is influenza, rhinovirus, respiratory syncytial virus, coronavirus and other upper respiratory viruses. This is why influenza vaccination is advised in asthma.

set2.q: Which statement about the course of asthma severity is accurate?
opts: Severe asthma is usually severe from onset

Correct. Severity rarely varies for a given patient: mild asthma rarely becomes severe, and severe asthma is usually severe at onset. Severity is thought to be largely genetic, which fits a stable course.
Mild asthma usually becomes severe over a decade

Mild asthma rarely becomes severe; severity tends to stay fixed for a patient. Symptoms can flare with triggers, but the underlying class rarely climbs. Tell: a steady march from mild to severe is the opposite of the stated course.
reversed direction or value
Severity changes with each season for most patients

Triggers such as pollen or cold air may cause seasonal flares, but the underlying severity rarely varies for a patient. Tell: a flare is a temporary worsening, while severity is the patient's stable baseline class.
common lay belief
Severity is set by the first viral infection in adulthood

No such rule is taught. Viral infections trigger exacerbations, and respiratory syncytial virus in infancy may be linked to developing asthma, but severity is likely genetic and rarely changes. Tell: severe asthma is usually severe at its onset, not after an adult infection.

set2.q: Asthma symptoms that occur at predictable times in the menstrual cycle are called which type?
opts: Cardiac asthma

Cardiac asthma is wheezing from decompensated heart failure. Symptoms tied to the menstrual cycle are catamenial asthma. Tell: cardiac asthma would come with signs of heart failure, not a monthly pattern.
competing diagnosis
Catamenial asthma

Correct. Catamenial asthma is asthma whose symptoms occur at predictable times during the menstrual cycle. It is listed among the other types of asthma with occupational, cardiac, exercise-induced and aspirin-sensitive patterns.
Intrinsic asthma

Intrinsic asthma is non-atopic, adult-onset and often has nasal polyps; it is defined by negative allergy testing, not by the menstrual cycle. Tell: timing to the cycle is the clue to catamenial asthma.
adjacent fact
Occupational asthma

Occupational asthma follows workplace exposure and improves on weekends and vacations. Symptoms timed to the menstrual cycle are catamenial asthma. Tell: occupational asthma follows a weekly work rhythm, not a monthly hormonal one.
competing diagnosis

set2.q: Which three conditions form the atopic triad?
opts: Allergic rhinitis, asthma, and atopic dermatitis

Correct. The atopic triad is allergic rhinitis, asthma and atopic dermatitis (eczema). Finding one prompts questions about the others, and in extrinsic asthma the exam may show swollen nasal mucosa, increased secretions or eczema even when the chest is clear.
Asthma, nasal polyps, and aspirin sensitivity

Nasal polyps and aspirin sensitivity accompany intrinsic asthma, which is non-atopic with negative skin tests. The atopic triad is allergic rhinitis, asthma and atopic dermatitis. Tell: a non-atopic cluster cannot be the atopic triad.
adjacent fact
Asthma, eczema, and food poisoning

Food poisoning is an acute infection, not an allergic condition. The triad is allergic rhinitis, asthma and atopic dermatitis (eczema). Tell: the triad members are allergic conditions; food poisoning is not.
common lay belief
Allergic rhinitis, sinusitis, and conjunctivitis

These are upper airway and eye problems, but the triad that defines atopy is allergic rhinitis, asthma and atopic dermatitis. Tell: the triad spans three organs, nose, lungs and skin, and asthma is one of the three.
adjacent fact

set2.q: Which is a side effect of systemic corticosteroids?
opts: Gastric ulceration

Correct. Systemic corticosteroid side effects include truncal obesity, osteoporosis, bruising, gastric ulcerations, depression and hypertension, which is why long-term use is kept to the minimum dose for refractory disease.
Oropharyngeal candidiasis

Oral thrush is a local effect of inhaled corticosteroids, prevented by a spacer and rinsing the mouth. Gastric ulceration is a systemic steroid effect. Tell: thrush comes from steroid deposited in the mouth, not from a swallowed or injected course.
adjacent fact
Hypokalemia with seizures

Hypokalemia and seizures are listed as theophylline toxicity. Gastric ulceration is among the systemic corticosteroid effects. Tell: seizures and low potassium belong to the drug with a narrow toxic-therapeutic range.
confused mechanism or drug class
Dry mouth

Dry mouth is the main adverse effect of the anticholinergic class. Systemic steroids cause ulcers, bruising, osteoporosis, truncal obesity, depression and hypertension. Tell: dry mouth reflects blocked cholinergic secretion, not a steroid effect.
confused mechanism or drug class

set2.q: What does fractional exhaled nitric oxide testing identify in asthma?
opts: Hyperinflation

Hyperinflation from air trapping is seen on a chest radiograph. Fractional exhaled nitric oxide identifies airway inflammation. Tell: hyperinflation is an imaging finding about lung size, while nitric oxide is a marker in exhaled breath.
adjacent fact
Airway inflammation

Correct. Fractional exhaled nitric oxide testing identifies airway inflammation. It sits with the chest radiograph and allergy testing among the other tests, while allergy skin or blood testing identifies the allergen triggers.
Allergen triggers

Allergen triggers are found with skin or blood allergy testing. Fractional exhaled nitric oxide identifies airway inflammation. Tell: a breath test reports on the airway itself, while allergy testing reports on what the immune system reacts to.
adjacent fact
Bronchodilator reversibility

Reversibility is shown by spirometry before and after a bronchodilator, a 12% or greater rise in the 1-second volume. Exhaled nitric oxide identifies airway inflammation. Tell: reversibility needs two spirometry measurements, not a breath gas level.
adjacent fact

set2.q: Which antibody response drives the asthma symptoms of allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis?
opts: An immunoglobulin M response

Immunoglobulin M is not the response described. The drivers are immunoglobulin E and immunoglobulin G. Tell: the allergic component comes from immunoglobulin E, which an immunoglobulin M answer leaves out entirely.
adjacent fact
A vigorous immunoglobulin E and G response

Correct. Exposure to Aspergillus causes a vigorous immunoglobulin E and immunoglobulin G antibody response, leading to acute asthma symptoms or an exacerbation in a patient with asthma or cystic fibrosis.
An immunoglobulin A response at the mucosa

Immunoglobulin A is not the response named. The hypersensitivity involves vigorous immunoglobulin E and G production. Tell: immunoglobulin E is the allergy antibody, which is why this is called an allergic aspergillosis.
adjacent fact
Absent antibodies with normal immunity
The reaction is a vigorous antibody response, immunoglobulin E and G, not an absent one. Tell: a hypersensitivity is by definition an over-reaction, so it cannot run on missing antibodies.
reversed direction or value
